scope.start: 3a.2: R. Yochanan's rabbinic oath, answering the *kal va'chomer* about Sumakhos (3a opens mid-exchange)
scope.end: 4a.14: the search for the source of R. Chiya's *kal va'chomer*, through one witness and *gilgul shevuah*

sections.title: Sumakhos and the Oath: A Rabbinic *Takkanah* Against Grabbing
sections.gist: Continuing the question of why Sumakhos, who divides without an oath, would require one here: R. Yochanan says this oath is a rabbinic ordinance against seizing another's garment.

bullets.text: Answer to the *kal va'chomer*: the Mishnah can follow Sumakhos, because this oath is rabbinic, as R. Yochanan says.
R. Yochanan: the oath of two holding a garment is a *takkanat chakhamim*, so that not everyone will go and seize another's garment and say "It is mine."
So this oath is not a tool for finding the truth but a deterrent. Without it, anyone bold enough could grab a coat, claim it, and walk off with half.
Nobody can stage a dispute over when a calf was born. There an oath could only serve to find the truth, a use Sumakhos rejects, so he divides without one.

sections.title: Divide or Set Aside Until Elijah: The Rabbis, R. Yosi, the Storekeeper
sections.gist: Does dividing the garment fit the dispute over a deposit? The Rabbis' rule, R. Yosi's two proposed distinctions, and why the storekeeper case pays both claimants in full.

children.title: The Deposit of 100 and 200: "What Did the Swindler Lose?"
children.gist: The Gemara suggests the Mishnah contradicts R. Yosi, who sets aside the whole deposit so that a false claimant does not come away without loss.

bullets.text: Suggestion: the Mishnah does not follow R. Yosi, who holds that a case may not be decided in a way that leaves no deterrent for a false claimant (37a).
The case: two people deposited with one bailee, one 100 dinars and one 200. The bailee forgot whose was whose, and each claims the 200.
The Rabbis: each takes 100, and the remainder is set aside until Elijah comes (*yehei munach ad she'yavo Eliyahu*).
R. Yosi: "If so, what did the swindler lose?" The entire deposit is set aside until Elijah comes.
R. Yosi's move is leverage. Wanting his own 100 back, the liar may break and admit, while the honest party holds out. The cost: the honest party's money is held too.

Divide with an oath: no certain swindler

children.title: The Rabbis: Divide Where Both May Own, Set Aside Where One Does
children.gist: The Rabbis set aside the disputed 100 because it surely belongs to only one man; the garment may belong to both, so it is divided with an oath.

bullets.text: Counter: the Rabbis fare no better. The whole garment is in doubt, like the remaining 100, so it too should be set aside until Elijah comes.
Answer: those 100 dinars certainly belong to only one of them, so they are set aside. The garment may belong to both, so the Rabbis divide it with an oath.
The test: could the split be true? If it could, divide. If a split would be a patently false judgment, set the item aside and wait.

Tosafot: the sugya deals with items both parties have some hold on (both grasp the garment; the bailee holds the money for both). Where no one holds the item, the Gemara elsewhere says *kol de'alim gevar*.

children.title: R. Yosi: No Certain Swindler, or No Loss for the Swindler?
children.gist: By a *kal va'chomer*, R. Yosi should set the garment aside. The Gemara offers two distinctions, rejects the second for a bought garment, and keeps the first: here there may be no swindler at all.

bullets.text: *Kal va'chomer*: R. Yosi sets aside even the 100 that surely belongs to each man. Here the whole garment may belong to one of them, so all the more should it be set aside.
First answer: in the deposit case there is certainly a swindler. Here, who says there is one? Perhaps both lifted the garment at the same time.
Second answer: there, R. Yosi holds the swindler's own deposit to push him to admit. Here the swindler loses nothing if the garment is set aside, so it would not move him.
The second answer is rejected. It works for a found item, but in buying and selling both paid for the item. So the first answer stands: here it is not certain that anyone is lying.
The swindler does lose a hoped-for gain. But setting an item aside is a real lever only when it withholds something that is truly his.
Tosafot reads the two answers as two conditions for setting aside: a certain liar, and a real cost to him.

returns_to.note: Returns to R. Yosi's ruling in the deposit case to test the Mishnah against it

children.title: Storekeeper and Laborer: Why Both Swear and Collect
children.gist: A case with a certain swindler where the money is not set aside: each claimant deals only with the employer, who trusted both without witnesses, so both swear and collect from him.

bullets.text: Question for both the Rabbis and R. Yosi: an employer told a storekeeper to give his laborer food in place of wages. The storekeeper says he gave it; the laborer says he got nothing. Per the mishnah (Shevuot 45a), each swears and collects from the employer.
Why not take the money from the employer and set it aside until Elijah comes? Surely one of them is a swindler.

The storekeeper can say: I carried out your agency and deal only with you. What business do I have with the laborer? Even if he swears, he is not trustworthy to me. You trusted him, since you did not tell me to give him food in front of witnesses.
The laborer can say: I worked for you. What relationship do I have with the storekeeper? Even if he swears, he is not trustworthy to me. So both swear and collect from the employer.
This is neither dividing nor setting aside. The employer set up an arrangement with no protection, and he bears the loss on both sides.

sections.title: R. Chiya's Baraita: Do Witnesses to Part of a Claim Obligate an Oath?
sections.gist: R. Chiya derives an oath from witnesses to part of a claim by *kal va'chomer* from *modeh be'miktzat*. The Gemara links it to the Mishnah, explains why the inference is needed, tests it against what only admission does, and looks for a new source in one witness.

children.title: Witnesses to 50: Pay 50, Swear on the Rest
children.gist: A claim of 100, a full denial, and witnesses to 50: he pays 50 and swears on the rest, since his own admission should not count for more than witnesses.

bullets.text: R. Chiya's baraita: "You have my 100"; "I have nothing of yours"; witnesses testify he owes 50. He pays 50 and swears about the rest.
Source: a *kal va'chomer* from *modeh be'miktzat*, one who admits part of a claim and must swear on the rest. His own admission should not carry more weight than the testimony of witnesses.
Unlike the rabbinic oath of the garment, the oath of *modeh be'miktzat* is biblical. R. Chiya's baraita extends it to part proved by witnesses.

children.title: The Mishnah as a Parallel: Each One's Grasp Counts as Witnesses
children.gist: The Gemara reads the Mishnah as the same law: what each holds is clearly his, like witnesses to part of his claim, and each swears.

bullets.text: The Mishnah taught the same: two hold a garment, each says "I found it", each swears and they divide.
Since each holds part, it is clear that what is in each one's grasp is his. That is like witnesses to part of each claim, and each still swears.

The comparison is strange: this "testimony" comes before the claims, and it cuts both ways at once. Still, it gives a path to reading the Mishnah's oath as the biblical one for part proved by evidence.

children.title: Why the Inference Is Needed: Rabba on the Debtor Who Won't Deny All
children.gist: By Rabba's explanation, partial admission reveals a debtor who is stalling rather than stealing, which an oath can move. A man proved liable only by witnesses might be wholly dishonest, so the *kal va'chomer* is needed.

bullets.text: Why is the *kal va'chomer* needed? So you won't say that the Torah imposes an oath only on one's own admission, as Rabba explains it.

Rabba: there is a presumption, *ein adam me'iz panav bifnei ba'al chovo*: a person is not brazen before his creditor, who did him a favor. He would like to deny everything but cannot bring himself to.
He would really like to admit it all, but he has no money now. He thinks: I'll put him off until I have the money, then pay it all. So the Torah imposes an oath, to bring him to admit it all.
When witnesses make him liable for part, this reasoning doesn't apply. Perhaps he never means to repay and his oath is worthless. So the baraita teaches the oath by *kal va'chomer*.
Rashi: the restraint comes from the favor of the loan. Tosafot: it applies even to *shevuat ha'shomrim*, where there was no favor, so it is a general reluctance to lie to someone's face.

An oath works here because it breaks through self-deception, much like honest *cheshbon ha'nefesh*. Against a total denier it may still work: he too may be stalling, or *chashud a'mamona lo chashud a'shevuata*.

children.title: Testing the Kal Va'chomer: Fines, Offerings, the Fifth, and *Hazamah*
children.gist: The inference is rephrased around fines, then challenged by what only admission does: offerings, the guilt-offering and the added fifth (answered through R. Meir), and immunity from contradiction and *hazamah*, which is left standing.

chart.caption: What one's own admission and two witnesses each accomplish, as the challenges to R. Chiya lay it out

children.title: Stating It: Admission Doesn't Obligate a *Kenas*, Witnesses Do
children.gist: First phrased as "admission doesn't obligate money", the inference is corrected, since admission is like 100 witnesses, to "admission doesn't obligate a fine".

bullets.text: The *kal va'chomer*: admission, which does not obligate money, obligates an oath. Witnesses, who do obligate money, all the more so.
Objection: admission doesn't obligate money? *Hoda'at ba'al din ke'me'ah edim*: a litigant's admission is like 100 witnesses.
Answer: the money meant is a *kenas*. One who admits to an act that carries a fine is exempt from it, while witnesses obligate him. The *kal va'chomer* is restated on that basis.
The argument is formal. It ranks the two kinds of evidence and ignores the psychology Rabba gave for the oath.
A fine, such as a thief's double payment, is a punishment rather than a debt, so like other punishments it needs outside witnesses.

children.title: Offerings: R. Meir vs. the Rabbis on Witnesses to Forbidden Fat
children.gist: Admission obligates an offering and witnesses may not. The Gemara answers that R. Chiya holds like R. Meir, who obligates an offering on witnesses' testimony by his own *kal va'chomer*.

bullets.text: Refutation: admission is weightier in one way. One who admits an unwitting sin brings an offering, while witnesses do not obligate him if he denies it.
Answer: R. Chiya holds like R. Meir, who says witnesses obligate an offering by *kal va'chomer*.
Mishnah (Keritot 11b): two witnesses say "You ate forbidden fat" and he says "I did not." R. Meir: liable to an offering. The Rabbis: exempt.

R. Meir: if two witnesses can bring him to the severe death penalty, can't they bring him to a light offering? The Rabbis: what if he wanted to say "I sinned intentionally"? No offering comes for that, so the witnesses cannot obligate one.
The Rabbis see an offering as resting on the sinner's own acknowledgment, much like *viduy*, which witnesses cannot supply. R. Meir sees it as a response to the sin itself, whatever the sinner says.

children.title: The Guilt-Offering and the Added Fifth: Also Following R. Meir
children.gist: Two more powers of admission, the robber's guilt-offering and the added fifth, are answered the same way: R. Chiya follows R. Meir.

bullets.text: Refutation: admission obligates a robber to bring a guilt-offering, while witnesses do not. Answer: a guilt-offering is like any offering, and R. Meir and the Rabbis dispute it.

Refutation: one who admits to wrongly holding another's money and returns it adds a fifth (Vayikra 5:20–26); with witnesses he does not. Answer: R. Chiya follows R. Meir, who also obligates the fifth by *kal va'chomer* when witnesses testify.

children.title: Admission Can't Be Contradicted or Refuted by *Hazamah*
children.gist: A final refutation goes unanswered: witnesses can be contradicted and refuted, while an admission cannot, so in some ways witnesses are weaker.

bullets.text: Refutation: an admission is not subject to contradiction or to *hazamah*, since witnesses cannot negate a litigant's own admission. Witnesses are subject to both.
So witnesses are weaker than admission in some respects. The Gemara does not answer this, and turns to a different source for R. Chiya's oath.

children.title: A New Source: One Witness, Then *Gilgul Shevuah*
children.gist: Having dropped admission as the source, the Gemara derives R. Chiya's oath from one witness, then Rav Pappa from the extension of that witness's oath, and then from admission and one witness together.

children.title: One Witness Obligates an Oath: Why Not Two?
children.gist: One witness, who cannot obligate money, obligates an oath, so all the more should two. This is rejected: the oath comes in on a different part of the claim.

bullets.text: *Kal va'chomer*: one witness, who does not obligate money, obligates an oath to contradict him. Two witnesses, who do obligate money, all the more so.
Rejected: with one witness, the defendant swears about the very matter the witness testified to. With two witnesses, he swears about the part he denies, not about the debt they testified to.

children.title: Rav Pappa: *Gilgul Shevuah*, Then Admission and One Witness Together
children.gist: Rav Pappa derives the oath from *gilgul shevuah*. When that is rejected, admission and one witness are combined, each answering the weakness of the other.

bullets.text: Rav Pappa: derive it from the extension of an oath (*gilgul shevuah*). Once one witness obligates an oath, the plaintiff can have other claims added to it.
Rejected: there one oath brings on another, and the witness does not cause the second oath directly. Witnesses make him liable to pay part, and liability to pay does not extend to the rest.
Response: admission shows that something other than an oath can bring an oath on the rest of the claim. One witness shows that even testimony open to contradiction can obligate an oath.

children.continues: The Gemara goes on to examine this combined derivation for R. Chiya's oath.

key_terms.definition: An enactment instituted by the Sages, rather than a law of the Torah, to meet a practical or social need.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Yochanan calls the oath of two holding a garment a rabbinic ordinance against seizing another's garment, which is why even Sumakhos can require it.

key_terms.sense: holding disputed property until the doubt is resolved
key_terms.definition: A court's ruling that property of unresolvable ownership is set aside and given to no one "until Elijah comes" to clarify the truth.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Rabbis set aside only the disputed 100 in the deposit case, R. Yosi the whole deposit; the Gemara explains why the garment is divided instead and why the storekeeper case pays both.

key_terms.sense: a defendant who admits part of a claim
key_terms.definition: A defendant who admits part of the claim against him and denies the rest; by Torah law he pays what he admits and swears about the remainder.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Chiya derives an oath for one proved liable for part by witnesses from this law, and Rabba explains why the Torah imposes the oath here.

key_terms.definition: An argument from a lighter case to a weightier one: if a law applies where the grounds are weaker, it applies all the more where they are stronger. It fails if the lighter case turns out to have a feature the weightier one lacks.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Several are run and tested: on Sumakhos, on R. Yosi, R. Chiya's from admission to witnesses, R. Meir's on offerings, and the attempts from one witness.

key_terms.term: ein adam me'iz panav bifnei ba'al chovo
key_terms.hebrew: אין אדם מעיז פניו בפני בעל חובו
key_terms.sense: a debtor won't brazenly deny a loan to his creditor's face
key_terms.definition: The presumption that a borrower will not have the nerve to deny the entire loan to the face of the creditor who lent it to him.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rabba uses it to explain why partial admission marks a debtor who is stalling, whom an oath can bring to admit everything.
aliases: ein adam me'iz panav bifnei ba'al chovo

key_terms.sense: a fine set by the Torah
key_terms.definition: A payment the Torah imposes beyond actual damages, such as double payment. One who admits the act on his own is exempt from it; only witnesses can obligate it.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The *kal va'chomer* is restated around fines: admission does not obligate a fine, while witnesses do.

key_terms.sense: refuting witnesses as having been elsewhere
key_terms.definition: Refuting witnesses by testimony that they were somewhere else at the time of the event; the refuted witnesses are punished with what they tried to bring on the defendant.
key_terms.on_this_daf: An admission can be neither contradicted nor refuted this way, which shows that witnesses are weaker in some respects and sinks the inference from admission.

key_terms.sense: extending an oath to further claims
key_terms.definition: Once a defendant must swear on one claim, the plaintiff may add other claims to that oath, even ones that would not have obligated an oath by themselves.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Pappa tries to derive R. Chiya's oath from the extension of an oath that one witness obligates; this is rejected because there one oath leads to another.

judgment_calls: The storekeeper case (s6) is nested under the divide-or-set-aside discussion rather than made its own top-level section: the Gemara raises it as a challenge to both the Rabbis and R. Yosi on exactly that question.

R. Yosi's two answers and the rejection of the second are kept in one section (s5) rather than split into children, because the second answer is raised and withdrawn within three lines and the conclusion returns to the first.
The search for a new source (one witness, Rav Pappa) could be a separate top-level section; kept under R. Chiya's baraita (s7) because it is still about deriving his oath.

The four refutations from admission's unique powers are grouped under s11 with the formulation about fines, since all test the premise that witnesses outweigh admission; the fifth and the offering are split into separate children because the shiur covers only the first.
coverage_notes: The outline starts at 3a.2. Line 3a.1 (the end of the kal va'chomer about Sumakhos) and the essay's discussion of Ben Nanas and Sumakhos's 'financial association' belong to the previous daf's scope.
The shiur ends with R. Chiya aligning with R. Meir (3b.7–3b.9). Lines 3b.10–4a.14 are outlined from the text only and flagged.

The provided text of the next daf ran only through 4a.4. The last section is anchored to 4a.14 as instructed, but its bullets describe only 4a.1–4a.4; the author should check 4a.5–4a.14 and fill in its content.
The essay calls the second answer for R. Yosi (the swindler loses nothing) 'arguably more decisive'. The text (3a.9) rejects it for bought items and returns to the first answer. Followed the text.

The essay says the Rabbis reject R. Meir because an offering requires viduy. The text gives their argument as 'what if he would want to say: I sinned intentionally?' Followed the text; the viduy framing is kept as the lecturer's reading (source: shiur).

The essay says the Gemara does not resolve the difficulty that Rabba's explanation raises for witnesses. The text (3b.2) says that is precisely why the baraita teaches the oath by kal va'chomer. Followed the text.

The essay's summary says no oath is given where one of the oaths is certainly false, 'as in the chanvani scenario'. The text says both the storekeeper and the laborer swear and collect. Followed the text.

The essay treats R. Chiya's alignment with R. Meir as the resolution. The text continues with further refutations, leaves the hazamah refutation unanswered, and turns to one witness. Followed the text.

The essay's example of a thief's double payment (kefel) and its mention of Rashi's reading of the Mishnah ('I wove it') are not in these lines. The first is kept as a shiur illustration; the second is omitted.
